title: I built a paper-trading leaderboard for AI agents and humans. How would you judge records or game it?
author: Frodo_Baghodler
selftext:
Disclosure: I'm Bob, the founder of ApesTogether. We're doing the public launch today.

The part of AI trading that interests me most is what happens after the backtest. Can a strategy keep doing well when it has to commit to trades before it knows the outcome?

I built a public paper-trading leaderboard where people trade through an iOS or Android app and bots submit trades through a REST API or MCP server. The server sets fill prices and timestamps the trades. Users can't remove individual filled trades from their record, and performance is compared with the S&P 500.

A bot could have a great few weeks because one big bet happened to work out, and the board could give the wrong impression if people delete the accounts that did badly. Even with a longer record, you'd still have to consider whether those paper fills were realistic for someone trading real money.

Buys use the ask and sells use the bid. Viewers can also include an extra penny per share of slippage in the performance they see via a switch in the settings, although a fixed adjustment can't capture every effect of order size, liquidity or the delay before someone acts on an alert.

Browsing performance is free. There are paid subscriptions for holdings and trade alerts, so I have a particular reason to care about this: I don't want someone paying for a record that looks more convincing than it is.

For those of you running trading bots, what would you measure alongside returns versus the S&P to judge whether a short record shows an edge? I'm especially interested in how you'd account for market exposure and drawdowns.

And how would you try to game a leaderboard with these rules?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Three things I'd put next to the S&P line, from running paper bots of my own.

Concentration: the share of the total that comes from the top five or ten trades. One of my paper bots has ten trades that add up to more than its whole total, so everything else it did nets to a loss. A return number hides that completely.

Survivors: show the count of accounts ever opened beside the count on the board, and keep a deleted account's record visible as closed. Otherwise the board is a list of whoever got lucky and stayed.

Size: a penny a share is fine for 100 shares of SPY and means nothing for an option or a thin name. Flag any fill bigger than a small slice of that minute's volume instead of adjusting it.

To game it as it stands I'd open ten accounts with opposite bets and keep the winner.

replies.author: Frodo_Baghodler
replies.body:
Those are great points. Currently you get 1 shot, so people only get a single account associated with their Apple or Android credentials. It's possible to make more than one but a pain. I can start watching IPs if needed but I really want people to try their best, not just throw a hundred back tested strategies against the wall. I think as the subscriber base grows and the subscription money involved becomes bigger, it will become more tempting to try and open the ten accounts.

For concentration, I think that's a great idea and I'll see what that looks like. I think it'd be very valuable for a lot of strategies, but maybe not all. My personal AI trader has strict filters for momentum so I'm often in 0-2 positions at a given time. Picking those good ones can set you above the S&P if you have good enough rules to make it consistent.

Size correction, I'll see what that looks like too. It's true that 1 tick slippage isn't ideal.

Thanks QuanTradin!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: one account per device login covers most of it. the other half is keeping a blown-up account on the board as a closed row. Quantradin is my take on the same idea, I built it for agents trading stocks and options on fake money, and the dead bots staying visible taught me more than the winners. quantradin.com

replies.author: Frodo_Baghodler
replies.body: That's a good idea. I haven't seen much in the way of blown accounts just yet but I'm sure I will lol

comments.author: alittlebitnostalgic
comments.body: we have to see how it handles a bad market than how much it makes during a good one. A few lucky trades can make anyone look like a genius. we should  see the drawdowns and how it performs over a longer period.

replies.author: Frodo_Baghodler
replies.body: That's a fact. I think last week revealed a bit but I have a feeling we'll be seeing more drawdowns soon. That will set apart the smart traders from the over leveraged.

replies.author: extraordinaire78
replies.body: I believe that using paper trading for about 3 months should be sufficient to at least try with a small account. The challenge that I find is that I get ideas to adjust my strategy and anything that is positive in my backtesting I immediately wish to try out. Its fustrating that when you get an idea that you think would work only to backtest it and find out it doesn't and don't get me started on other people's strategies. Read, learn how to trade manually then automate.

comments.author: pigeon_shit
comments.body:
Congrats on the launch. Before I’d trust a record on this, I’d want to know:

* Can a user delete a whole account, or only single trades? If they can, a leaderboard is easy to game.
* Are paid alerts sent before or after the fill is locked in? If they go out first, subscribers can act on trades that never settle.
* How do you keep one agent’s API key or MCP connection from reading another’s orders?
* Do paid alerts carry a not-advice disclaimer, and what do you say to users who copy them with real money?
* Is the timestamping audited by anyone outside the app?

The “how would you judge it” question is the harder one to answer.

replies.author: Frodo_Baghodler
replies.body:
Thanks pigeon_shit lol. It took over a year and a pivot along the way. Users can only delete their entire account, not individual trades, and because you can only sign in through Apple or Google it's kind of a pain to have any more than a single account. That's set up to discourage people from running tons of back tested strategies and encourage only bringing the one ready for showtime.

Alerts come after the fill, though since it's paper trading it's a theoretical fill at the bid or ask.

The particular API key is associated with a single authenticated account. MCP uses the same authenticates API handler and permissions.

The paid alerts carry the not advice disclaimer which is also well covered in the TOS at signup. We don't encourage or tell anyone how to copy the trades with real money. 

We don't have 3rd party auditing of the timestamps right now.

Yeah, the question of how to judge may be more geared towards potential subscribers than creators.

replies.author: pigeon_shit
replies.body: Appreciate the straight answers, that’s more than most launches give. Makes sense that judging a record is more of a subscriber problem than a creator one. Curious what subscribers actually ask you before they pay? I build my own trading bots and I’m trying to learn what makes a track record believable to someone paying for it. If you’re up for swapping notes, DM me. Happy to share what I’ve found on my side, method stuff only.

replies.author: Frodo_Baghodler
replies.body: Same and that's why I'm here lol. I don't do much in the way of outreach, I kinda put it to market and let people decide under the general assumption that people want alternatives to expensive Discords and copy trading platforms. I sent an email soliciting that info from my current users and what little response I got was sparse and generally not actionable. Maybe I should run ads with the comments turned on...

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
One more way to game it besides the opposite-bets accounts: go all in on high-variance stuff, and once you're near the top, stop trading. Any board ranked by total return rewards that. A rolling window for the ranking plus a minimum number of trades and active days kills most of it.

For exposure I'd show average gross exposure right next to the return. 10% made while 30% invested is a very different record than 10% at 300%. Return divided by max drawdown is also simple and people get it right away.
